title: connect
aim: Talk about communication, report speech and keep conversations going.

lessons.title: Mix-up
goals: See how one word causes misunderstanding

grammar.title: Reported speech
grammar.shortAr: نقل الكلام في الماضي يرجّع الزمن والضمائر؛ والسؤال بـ if/whether يأتي بترتيب خبرى.
points: Use a past reporting verb (said, told, asked) and move the verb one tense back.
Change pronouns and references: now → then, yesterday → the day before, here → there.
Yes/no questions use if/whether and statement word order; no question mark.
table: ‘I’m in a hurry.’ → Feisal said that he was in a hurry.
‘I speak Spanish.’ → Heidi told me that she spoke Spanish.
‘My phone has just broken.’ → Hakim complained that his phone had just broken.
‘Do you speak English?’ → She asked me if I spoke English.
exceptions: No backshift when the information is still true.

vocab.example: Did you read aloud at school?
Someone screamed ‘Help!’ in the street.
Do you shout at people when angry?
Would you speak up in a group?
If he whispers, do you whisper back?
Talk big decisions over with someone.

writing: Write a story about an event.

practice.q: ‘I’m in a hurry.’ → He said that he ___ in a hurry.
She asked me ___ I spoke English.
‘I’m working from home.’ → She explained that she ___ from home.

lessons.title: Oversharing

grammar.title: Passives
grammar.shortAr: المبني للمجهول: be + التصريف الثالث؛ يركّز على المفعول. get بديل غير رسمي للأحداث المفاجئة.
points: be + past participle focuses on the affected person or thing, not the doer.
Passive when the doer is obvious, unknown or unimportant; add by only if it matters.
Informal get + past participle is common for unexpected negative events.
table: English is spoken in most cities.
It was made over a thousand years ago.
The app has been downloaded over a million times.
exceptions: get is informal and usually negative.

vocab.example: Which icons can you name?
How often do you download files?
Do you name your folders clearly?
How many emails are in your inbox?
Press refresh for new information.
Swipe left or right on your phone.

listening.summary: Passive examples about being tagged and spammed.

speaking: Discuss issues connected to online privacy.

practice.q: The app ___ over a million times.

lessons.title: Conversation savers

grammar.title: How to keep a conversation going
grammar.shortAr: عبارات البداية والمتابعة والأسئلة القصيرة والتعليقات تبقي الحوار مستمراً.
points: Start: How do you know…? / Can you recommend…?
Continue: How did you get into that? What do you mean by…?
Short questions: Such as? Why’s that? And then? Comments: Sounds interesting!
table: How did you get into that?

vocab.example: I do UI animation, actually.
Obviously, you learn a lot about cooking.
This salad’s particularly nice.
This food’s extremely good.
I’d definitely go to help.
I’m probably a good communicator.

listening.summary: Short questions for examples and reasons.

writing: Write an email giving advice about a problem.

practice.q: You want an example. What do you ask?
practice.why: Such as? asks for an example.

practice.q: Which keeps a conversation going after ‘I worked at a café’?
options: How did that make you feel?
practice.answer: How did that make you feel?

practice.q: To ask about a reason, use:
practice.why: How come? asks for a reason.

grammar.title: Avoiding repetition: so, to, not, be
grammar.shortAr: نتجنّب التكرار بـ do/so/not/to/be بدل إعادة الجملة.
points: do/does/did replace a verb: I didn’t see John, but Mary did.
so/not: I think so, I hope not, I don’t think so.
After want, would like and try, keep to or to be: Yes, I’d love to.
exceptions: Prefer don’t think so to think not.

vocab.example: Are you going? — I think so.
We’ll miss the plane. — I hope not.
Can I borrow it? — I suppose so.
Come with us. — I’d love to.
Don’t work too hard. — I’ll try not to.
Did she finish? — I don’t think so.
